```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(nlmixr2lib)
library(rxode2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

# Model and source

* Citation: `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Cirincione_2017_mealQT_24h"))$reference`
* Breakfast-window model: `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Cirincione_2017_mealQT_breakfast"))$description`
* 24-hour model: `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Cirincione_2017_mealQT_24h"))$description`
* Article: <https://doi.org/10.1002/jcph.933> (open access, PMC5518218)

Cirincione 2017 describes how a meal changes the QT interval on a drug-free
baseline day. Meal carbohydrate raises plasma glucose. The change in glucose
stimulates the production of heart rate (HR) in an indirect-response model,
and the predicted RR interval shortens QT through a power-law QT-RR
relationship. A further delayed glucose effect, through one
signal-transduction compartment, shortens QT beyond what the change in HR
explains.

The authors fitted the model twice. The **breakfast-window model** covers the
richly sampled period from 6 am to 2 pm. The **24-hour model** covers the
whole baseline day, with a two-harmonic circadian rhythm on HR production.
In the 24-hour model the glucose-to-QT delay parameters (`ktr`, `STR`) are
fixed to their breakfast-window estimates. Both are packaged, as
`Cirincione_2017_mealQT_breakfast` and `Cirincione_2017_mealQT_24h`.

No drug is involved. The study was run to design a thorough QT study of an
antidiabetic agent, where a drug that lowers postprandial glucose could
remove part of this meal effect and confound the comparison with placebo.

# Population

Twenty-one healthy adults enrolled in an open-label phase 1 pilot study in
three cohorts (A, n = 6; B, n = 6; C, n = 9). One subject was removed for an
abnormal postprandial glucose profile, leaving 20 (Results, "Baseline Subject
PD and Demographics"). They were 95% male and 85% white, with mean (SD) age
40.0 (12.4) years and weight 91.2 (12.1) kg. Subjects received a standardized
2500 kcal/day diet. Breakfast was at 7 am (cohort A) or 6 am (cohorts B and
C) and lunch at 2 pm. Breakfast carbohydrate was 81, 86 and 99 g, and lunch
190, 144 and 104 g, for cohorts A, B and C. The carbohydrate amount, scaled by
the fraction of the meal eaten, was used as the apparent glucose dose.
Holter ECGs were read hourly (every 30 minutes around breakfast), and plasma
glucose was measured at 14 times.

The same information is available programmatically via
`readModelDb("Cirincione_2017_mealQT_24h")()$population`.

# Source trace

Every `ini()` value carries an in-file comment pointing to its source.

| Equation / parameter | Breakfast | 24 hours | Source location |
|----------------------|-----------|----------|-----------------|
| `d/dt(glucose) = ka_glu/Vg * depot + Kin_glu - kout_glu * glucose` | n/a | n/a | Eq. 1 |
| `Kin_glu = kout_glu * Gluss` | n/a | n/a | Methods, text after Eq. 1 |
| `d/dt(hr) = Kin_HR * (1 + SHR * (glucose - Gluss)) - kout_HR * hr` | n/a | n/a | Eq. 2 |
| `... * (1 + CIRC)` on HR production | none | n/a | Eq. 9 |
| `Kin_HR = kout_HR * HRss` | n/a | n/a | Eq. 3 |

| `d/dt(effect) = ktr * (glucose - Gluss - effect)` | n/a | n/a | Eq. 7 |

# Models

```{r models}
mod_bf <- readModelDb("Cirincione_2017_mealQT_breakfast")
mod_24 <- readModelDb("Cirincione_2017_mealQT_24h")
```

Doses are meal carbohydrate in mg (grams times 1000) into `depot`.
Observation rows use the `glucose` state, and rxode2 returns `hr`, `qt`,
`qtc_hr` (mQTc) and `qtc_hr_glucose` (mQTcG) at every row. In the
breakfast-window model time 0 is 6 am. In the 24-hour model time 0 is 8 pm,
the start of the baseline day, and the cosines read `t` directly.

# Structural checks

## Steady state without a meal

Without a meal and without circadian variation, the breakfast-window model
must hold glucose at `Gluss`, HR at `HRss` and QT at
`QTint * (60 / HRss)^alpha`.

```{r steady-state}
ev_none <- rxode2::et(seq(0, 8, by = 0.5), cmt = "glucose")
ss <- rxode2::rxSolve(rxode2::zeroRe(mod_bf), ev_none, returnType = "data.frame")
qt_ss <- 406 * (60 / 64.3)^0.362
stopifnot(
  max(abs(ss$glucose - 90)) < 1e-6,
  max(abs(ss$hr - 64.3)) < 1e-6,
  max(abs(ss$qt - qt_ss)) < 1e-6
)
c(glucose = ss$glucose[1], hr = ss$hr[1], qt = ss$qt[1])
```

## Glucose against its closed form

The glucose sub-model is linear: a first-order input into a one-compartment
pool on top of a constant baseline. Above baseline it must match the
one-compartment oral closed form
`D / Vg * ka / (ka - k) * (exp(-k t) - exp(-ka t))`. Both sides use the same
typical values, so the bound is a numerical-error bound.

```{r glucose-closed-form}
ev_meal <- rxode2::et(seq(0, 8, by = 0.05), cmt = "glucose") |>
  rxode2::et(time = 0, amt = 99000, cmt = "depot")
typ24 <- rxode2::rxSolve(rxode2::zeroRe(mod_24), ev_meal, returnType = "data.frame")
ka <- 1.72; k <- 1.94; vg <- 653
closed <- 99000 / vg * ka / (ka - k) * (exp(-k * typ24$time) - exp(-ka * typ24$time))
stopifnot(max(abs((typ24$glucose - 92.8) - closed)) < 1e-3)
c(
  peak_rise_mg_dL = max(typ24$glucose - 92.8),
  time_of_peak_h = typ24$time[which.max(typ24$glucose)]
)
```

The typical-value rise of about 52.5 mg/dL at about 33 minutes matches the paper's
predicted maximum mean change in glucose, 52.2 mg/dL (95% CI 50.6-53.7),
30 minutes after a 99 g breakfast (Results, "PD Modeling: 24-Hour Model").

# Replicate Figure 5: fed versus fasted day (24-hour model)

The paper simulated 500 subjects through a fasted 24-hour day and a fed day
with a 99 g carbohydrate breakfast at 7 am. Each subject appears in both
scenarios. Here 200 subjects are used. Re-seeding before each solve gives
both scenarios the same random effects, which the check below confirms.

Starting HR at its 8 pm value, `HRss * (1 + CIRC(0))`, is not the periodic
steady state of the circadian rhythm. The simulation therefore runs a 24-hour
fasted run-in day first and plots the second day (model time 24-48 h).
Breakfast at 7 am on the second day is model time 35 h.

```{r figure5-sim}
tg <- seq(0, 48, by = 0.5)
ev_fast <- rxode2::et(tg, cmt = "glucose")
ev_fed <- rxode2::et(tg, cmt = "glucose") |>
  rxode2::et(time = 35, amt = 99000, cmt = "depot")

rxode2::rxSetSeed(2017)
s_fed <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod_24, ev_fed, nSub = 200, returnType = "data.frame")
rxode2::rxSetSeed(2017)
s_fast <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod_24, ev_fast, nSub = 200, returnType = "data.frame")
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(
  s_fed$rbase_hr[s_fed$time == 0], s_fast$rbase_hr[s_fast$time == 0]
)))

day2 <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  dplyr::mutate(s_fed, scenario = "Fed"),
  dplyr::mutate(s_fast, scenario = "Fasting")
) |>
  dplyr::filter(time >= 24) |>
  dplyr::rename(id = sim.id) |>
  dplyr::mutate(clock = time - 24 + 20)

fig5_summary <- day2 |>
  dplyr::group_by(scenario, clock) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    hr_mean = mean(hr), hr_se = sd(hr) / sqrt(dplyr::n()),
    qt_mean = mean(qt), qt_se = sd(qt) / sqrt(dplyr::n()),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r figure5ab, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 6}
fig5_summary |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    c(hr_mean, qt_mean), names_to = "endpoint", values_to = "mean"
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    se = ifelse(endpoint == "hr_mean", hr_se, qt_se),
    endpoint = ifelse(endpoint == "hr_mean", "A: HR (bpm)", "B: QT (ms)")
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(clock, mean, colour = scenario)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - se, ymax = mean + se), width = 0.2) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~endpoint, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(20, 44, by = 2),
    labels = function(x) x %% 24
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Clock time (h)", y = "Mean (SE)", colour = NULL,
    caption = "Replicates Figure 5A and 5B of Cirincione 2017."
  )
```

```{r figure5cd, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 6}
fed_chg <- day2 |>
  dplyr::filter(scenario == "Fed", clock >= 30, clock <= 38) |>
  dplyr::group_by(id) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    d_hr = hr - hr[clock == 30],
    d_glucose = glucose - glucose[clock == 30],
    d_qt = qt - qt[clock == 30],
    d_qtc = qtc_hr - qtc_hr[clock == 30],
    d_qtcg = qtc_hr_glucose - qtc_hr_glucose[clock == 30]
  ) |>
  dplyr::ungroup() |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    c(d_hr, d_glucose, d_qt, d_qtc, d_qtcg),
    names_to = "quantity", values_to = "change"
  ) |>
  dplyr::group_by(quantity, clock) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    mean = mean(change), se = sd(change) / sqrt(dplyr::n()),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    panel = ifelse(
      quantity %in% c("d_hr", "d_glucose"),
      "C: change in HR (bpm) and glucose (mg/dL)",
      "D: change in QT, mQTc, mQTcG (ms)"
    ),
    quantity = dplyr::recode(
      quantity,
      d_hr = "HR", d_glucose = "Glucose", d_qt = "QT",
      d_qtc = "mQTc", d_qtcg = "mQTcG"
    )
  )

ggplot(fed_chg, aes(clock - 24, mean, colour = quantity)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - se, ymax = mean + se), width = 0.1) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~panel, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    x = "Clock time (h)", y = "Mean (SE) change from 6 am", colour = NULL,
    caption = "Replicates Figure 5C and 5D of Cirincione 2017 (fed scenario)."
  )
```

## Comparison with the published simulation

HR is linear in `SHR` once the other random effects are fixed, so the
population-mean HR curve equals the curve solved at the mean of `SHR`,
`theta * exp(omega^2 / 2)`. Solving at that value removes the noisiest
random effect from the check. `SHR` has 140% IIV, and its log-normal tail
makes a 200-subject mean HR wander by about 0.7 bpm. The QT interval is not
linear in HR, so the QT values below come from the full simulation above.

```{r mean-shr}
omega_shr <- rxode2::rxode(mod_24)$omega["etalsstim_glucose_hr", "etalsstim_glucose_hr"]
mod_24_meanshr <- rxode2::rxode(mod_24) |>
  rxode2::model(sstim_glucose_hr <- exp(lsstim_glucose_hr))
rxode2::rxSetSeed(2017)
s_mean <- rxode2::rxSolve(
  mod_24_meanshr, ev_fed, nSub = 200, returnType = "data.frame",
  params = c(lsstim_glucose_hr = log(0.00103) + omega_shr / 2)
)
mean_hr <- s_mean |>
  dplyr::group_by(time) |>
  dplyr::summarise(hr = mean(hr), glucose = mean(glucose), .groups = "drop")
base6 <- mean_hr[mean_hr$time == 34, ]
hr_rise <- max(mean_hr$hr - base6$hr)
hr_rise_t <- mean_hr$time[which.max(mean_hr$hr - base6$hr)] - 35
glu_rise <- max(mean_hr$glucose - base6$glucose)

fed_mean <- fed_chg |>
  dplyr::group_by(quantity) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    # Breakfast at model time 35 h is clock 31 on the shifted axis
    min = min(mean), t_min = clock[which.min(mean)] - 31,
    max = max(mean), .groups = "drop"
  )
qt_drop <- fed_mean$min[fed_mean$quantity == "QT"]
qt_drop_t <- fed_mean$t_min[fed_mean$quantity == "QT"]
qtc_drop <- fed_mean$min[fed_mean$quantity == "mQTc"]
qtcg_range <- max(abs(unlist(fed_mean[fed_mean$quantity == "mQTcG", c("min", "max")])))

fast_hr <- fig5_summary |> dplyr::filter(scenario == "Fasting")
hr_min <- min(fast_hr$hr_mean)
hr_min_clock <- fast_hr$clock[which.min(fast_hr$hr_mean)] %% 24

claims <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Quantity, ~Published, ~Simulated,
  "Max mean glucose rise after 99 g (mg/dL)", "52.2 (50.6-53.7)", glu_rise,
  "Max mean HR rise from 6 am (bpm)", "6.8 (6.0-7.6)", hr_rise,
  "Time of max HR rise after the meal (h)", "1.5", hr_rise_t,
  "Max mean QT change from 6 am (ms)", "-24 (-22.4 to -25.5)", qt_drop,
  "Time of max QT change after the meal (h)", "2", qt_drop_t,
  "Max mean mQTc change from 6 am (ms)", "about -10", qtc_drop,
  "Largest mean mQTcG change from 6 am (ms)", "none", qtcg_range,
  "Fasting mean HR minimum (bpm, Figure 5A)", "about 59", hr_min,
  "Clock time of fasting HR minimum (h, Figure 5A)", "about 2", hr_min_clock
)
knitr::kable(claims, digits = 2)

stopifnot(
  # Glucose: the IIV on kout_glu barely moves the mean peak.
  abs(glu_rise - 52.2) < 2.6,
  # HR: the published 95% CI. Reading the Table 1 'IIV (%)' column as
  # log(1 + CV^2) instead gives about 5.5 bpm and fails this bound.
  hr_rise > 6.0, hr_rise < 7.6,
  abs(hr_rise_t - 1.5) <= 0.5,
  # QT: full-simulation means; realised -24.2 here, and the SHR tail moves
  # a 200-subject mean by about 1-2 ms between draws.
  qt_drop < -20, qt_drop > -30,
  abs(qt_drop_t - 2) <= 1,
  qtc_drop < -7, qtc_drop > -13,
  abs(hr_min - 59.2) < 2,
  hr_min_clock >= 1, hr_min_clock <= 3
)
```

mQTcG removes both the HR and the glucose terms. Its value is therefore
exactly `QTint` for every subject at every time, and the mean change is zero.

```{r qtcg-identity}
stopifnot(max(abs(s_fed$qtc_hr_glucose - s_fed$qtb)) < 1e-6)
```

# Breakfast-window model

The breakfast-window model has no circadian term and no IIV on `SHR`. Below,
100 subjects per cohort receive each cohort's breakfast: 81 g at 7 am
(cohort A), and 86 g or 99 g at 6 am (cohorts B and C). The bands are
5th-95th percentiles of the individual predictions (no residual error), and
the line is the median. They are for comparison with the observed medians of
Figure 2 and the visual predictive check of Figure 4 (top row).

```{r breakfast-sim, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 6}
make_cohort <- function(label, grams, meal_time, id_offset) {
  ev <- rxode2::et(seq(0, 8, by = 0.25), cmt = "glucose") |>
    rxode2::et(time = meal_time, amt = grams * 1000, cmt = "depot")
  rxode2::rxSetSeed(id_offset + 1)
  s <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod_bf, ev, nSub = 100, returnType = "data.frame")
  dplyr::mutate(s, id = as.integer(sim.id) + id_offset, cohort = label)
}
bf <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  make_cohort("A: 81 g at 7 am", 81, 1, 0L),
  make_cohort("B: 86 g at 6 am", 86, 0, 100L),
  make_cohort("C: 99 g at 6 am", 99, 0, 200L)
)

bf |>
  dplyr::select(cohort, time, Glucose = glucose, HR = hr, QT = qt) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(Glucose, HR, QT), names_to = "endpoint") |>
  dplyr::group_by(cohort, endpoint, time) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    lo = quantile(value, 0.05), med = median(value), hi = quantile(value, 0.95),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(time + 6, med)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_grid(endpoint ~ cohort, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    x = "Clock time (h)", y = "Glucose (mg/dL), HR (bpm), QT (ms)",
    caption = "Compare Figures 2 and 4 (top row) of Cirincione 2017."
  )
```

Typical-value responses for cohort C, from 6 am:

```{r breakfast-typical}
ev_c <- rxode2::et(seq(0, 8, by = 0.05), cmt = "glucose") |>
  rxode2::et(time = 0, amt = 99000, cmt = "depot")
typ_bf <- rxode2::rxSolve(rxode2::zeroRe(mod_bf), ev_c, returnType = "data.frame")
typ_tab <- tibble::tibble(
  Quantity = c(
    "Glucose rise (mg/dL)", "Time of glucose peak (h)",
    "HR rise (bpm)", "Time of HR peak (h)",
    "QT change (ms)", "mQTc change (ms)", "Time of mQTc nadir (h)"
  ),
  Value = c(
    max(typ_bf$glucose - 90), typ_bf$time[which.max(typ_bf$glucose)],
    max(typ_bf$hr - 64.3), typ_bf$time[which.max(typ_bf$hr)],
    min(typ_bf$qt - typ_bf$qt[1]), min(typ_bf$qtc_hr - typ_bf$qtc_hr[1]),
    typ_bf$time[which.min(typ_bf$qtc_hr)]
  )
)
knitr::kable(typ_tab, digits = 2)
```

The observed medians of Figure 2 show the glucose peak about 1 hour after
the meal and the HR peak about 2 hours after it, with an HR rise of about
10 bpm. They also show a transient fall in QTcF with its nadir about 3 hours
after the meal. The model peaks glucose earlier, at about 35 minutes,
because `ka_glu` is fixed. The paper notes that the model slightly
underpredicts the peak HR rise (Results, "PD Modeling: Breakfast Window").

# Assumptions and deviations

* **IIV scale.** Table 1 reports IIV as a percentage. Read as
  `100 * sqrt(omega^2)`, so `omega^2 = (IIV / 100)^2`, the 24-hour model
  reproduces the published 500-subject simulation. Its mean postprandial HR
  rise is 6.8-7.2 bpm against the published 6.8 bpm (95% CI 6.0-7.6). Read
  as the log-normal CV, `omega^2 = log(1 + CV^2)`, the rise is about 5.5 bpm,
  outside that interval. The difference comes almost entirely from the 140%
  IIV on `SHR`. The same reading is applied to the breakfast-window model.
* **Equation 8a sign.** Equation 8a defines the HR- and glucose-corrected QT
  as `(QT + STR * TR) / RR^alpha`. With QT from Equation 8b,
  `QTint * RR^alpha + STR * TR`, only `(QT - STR * TR) / RR^alpha` removes
  the glucose term and gives the flat mQTcG profile of Figure 5D ("no
  remaining change in mQTcG was observed across time"). The model uses the
  minus sign. This affects only the derived output `qtc_hr_glucose`, not
  the fitted endpoints.
* **Two glucose residual errors.** Table 1 lists "RV glucose" twice in each
  column: 9.18% and 8.78% (breakfast), 11% and 11.3% (24 hours). The glucose
  parameters were estimated first and then fixed at their individual Bayesian
  estimates while the HR and QT parts were fitted. The first row belongs to the
  glucose-only stage. The second row sits in the final residual block with
  RV HR and RV QT and is used here.
* **Initial conditions.** The authors set the initial glucose and HR to each
  subject's measured value at time zero. The packaged models start glucose at
  `Gluss` and HR at `HRss` (breakfast) or `HRss * (1 + CIRC(0))` (24 hours),
  and the signal-transduction state at 0 as in the paper. For the 24-hour
  model, run in one day without a meal to start from the periodic steady
  state. The published Figure 5A starts at about 66.9 bpm at 8 pm, close to
  this model's periodic value at 8 pm and above the typical
  `HRss * (1 + CIRC(0))` of 65.3 bpm.
* **Glucose reference in Equation 9.** Equation 9 writes the glucose
  stimulus of the 24-hour model as `Glu - Glu0`, whereas Equation 2 writes
  `Glu - Gluss`. With glucose starting at `Gluss` the two coincide, and the
  model uses `Gluss`.
* **Time origin.** The paper references time in the 24-hour model to "the
  start of the baseline day", which began at 8 pm. The acrophases then place
  the fasting HR minimum near 2 am and the maximum near 6:30 pm, as Figure 5A
  shows. Reading them as clock times would put the minimum near 6 am. The
  breakfast-window model starts at 6 am, the time of its initial conditions.
* **Table 1 against the text.** The Discussion quotes the 24-hour `kout_HR`
  as 14.8 per day, and Table 1 gives 14.3. The breakfast-window text mentions
  an IIV on `SHR`, but Table 1 and the list of final IIV terms do not include
  one. The model follows Table 1 in both cases.
* **Units.** `kout_HR` is reported per day and is divided by 24 in `model()`.
  The carbohydrate dose is in mg (grams times 1000) with bioavailability 1,
  and `Vg` is in dL, so glucose is in mg/dL. RR is in seconds.
* **Not modelled.** The study measured insulin, but the authors dropped it
  from the model because a glucose-insulin feedback model was unstable on
  these data.
